item.title: ExecuTorch-TensorRT: PyTorch Robot Policies at NVIDIA TensorRT Speed

The post ExecuTorch-TensorRT: PyTorch Robot Policies at NVIDIA TensorRT Speed appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  • With Torch-TensorRT 2.15 and ExecuTorch 1.6 you can compile a PyTorch model with TensorRT, save it as an ExecuTorch program, and run it from C++ or Python without loading torch. You stay in PyTorch the whole way, and whatever TensorRT can’t handle can still run on the GPU.
  • On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano it comes within 4% of the fastest TensorRT setup we measured, in both speed and memory. A 3.6-billion-parameter policy fits on the 8 GB board, where PyTorch eager mode runs out of memory.
  • You compile with one pip install "torch_tensorrt[executorch]". To run, the robot needs only ExecuTorch and a small TensorRT backend, not PyTorch.

We talked about this work at PyTorch Conference 2026: Deploying Robot Policies Across Many Targets with ExecuTorch.

 

GR00T 1.7 (3B) on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB: about 200 ms per action chunk.

Why is it hard to run a PyTorch model with TensorRT on a robot?

A robot runs its models on its own computer, like NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor or a custom board, and they have to finish on time. A policy, the model that decides what the robot does next, returns a short plan at a time, called an action chunk, say 50 actions. If the next chunk isn’t ready when the robot finishes the current one, the robot stops and waits. And everything shares the same memory: the CPU, the GPU, the cameras and every model. Offloading to a server adds a network round trip, which can easily take 100 ms, over a link the robot can’t always count on.

On NVIDIA hardware the fastest way to run a model is TensorRT, NVIDIA’s inference compiler. Until now, getting a PyTorch model into TensorRT meant one of four things:

  • Go through ONNX. We call this ONNX-TensorRT in the tables. Export the model to an ONNX file and build a TensorRT engine from it. It’s fast and well proven, but your model has to get through two converters you don’t own: PyTorch’s ONNX exporter and TensorRT’s ONNX parser. If either one doesn’t know an op, the build fails, and the usual way out is writing a TensorRT plugin in C++.
  • Write it by hand. Rebuild the model layer by layer with TensorRT’s network definition API. tensorrtx does this for many popular models, and early TensorRT-LLM did it for language models. You get full control, but every new model is new work, and checking the result against PyTorch is on you.
  • Use TensorRT Model Connect. NVIDIA’s TensorRT Model Connect, in public preview, builds TensorRT engines straight from supported Hugging Face checkpoints, with no ONNX step, and runs them from C++ without PyTorch. It covers the models on its supported list.
  • Use Torch-TensorRT inside PyTorch. Torch-TensorRT converts PyTorch ops to TensorRT directly, no ONNX file involved. But what it normally produces, an ExportedProgram or an AOTInductor .pt2 package, needs libtorch to run. That’s more than 1 GB of libraries, and a process that loads it holds hundreds of MB that inference never uses.

The ONNX route and the ExecuTorch route.

Today we’re adding a new way: Torch-TensorRT 2.15 compiles the model with TensorRT and saves it as an ExecuTorch 1.6 program that runs without libtorch. It skips ONNX and captures the model with PyTorch’s own torch.export. If TensorRT can’t convert part of the model, preprocessing included, you can send that part to ExecuTorch’s CUDA backend, which runs it on the GPU in the same program on the same CUDA stream instead of failing the build. The TensorRT parts are ordinary TensorRT engines, so the model runs about as fast as it does when you call TensorRT directly.

How it works

ExecuTorch is PyTorch’s solution for running models on edge devices. You compile a model ahead of time into a program, and a small runtime runs it without libtorch, from C++ or Python. Hardware support comes from backends: besides TensorRT there are CUDA, Intel OpenVINO, Qualcomm QNN, Apple Core ML and MLX, Arm, Vulkan, and XNNPACK for CPUs. Torch-TensorRT could already save ExecuTorch programs with output_format="executorch". What’s new in Torch-TensorRT 2.15 and ExecuTorch 1.6 is that the workflow is production ready: one install, prebuilt C++ libraries, a Python runtime that doesn’t need PyTorch, and a few features for small boards. We call it ExecuTorch-TensorRT.

Take a toy model that needs two backends:

class Toy(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.cos(torch.erfinv(torch.tanh(x)))

 

The toy model, split across two backends.

  1. Capture and split. torch.export turns the model into a graph of PyTorch ops. TensorRT claims every part it can convert. It has no converter for erfinv, so the ExecuTorch CUDA backend takes that part instead. The compiler tells you which ops didn’t go to TensorRT, and why.
  2. Compile and pack. TensorRT builds an engine for each part it claimed, and the CUDA backend compiles its part with AOTInductor. The engines go into a .pte file, and the CUDA backend’s weights go into a .ptd data file next to it.
  3. Load and run. On the robot, the ExecuTorch runtime hands each part to its backend. Inputs, outputs and the tensors passed between the two backends can stay on the GPU, with no round trip through the CPU. If you set use_cuda_graphs=True, each engine’s GPU work is recorded once as a CUDA graph and replayed with a single launch, which makes every call cheaper.

If your model has a custom op that neither TensorRT nor the CUDA backend can compile, you still don’t need a TensorRT plugin in C++. Write the op as a Triton kernel and register it with torch.library.triton_op. The CUDA backend compiles it into the program like any other part of the model, and the robot runs it without Triton or PyTorch installed. ExecuTorch’s own CUDA kernels for attention, mixture-of-experts layers and 4-bit matmuls are written this way.

Getting started

Install

pip install "torch_tensorrt[executorch]"

That gets you PyTorch, Torch-TensorRT, ExecuTorch and a small TensorRT backend for ExecuTorch. You need PyTorch only to compile. The compiled program runs without it; see Run, in Python, without torch for the smaller install for the robot. The wheels are built for CUDA 13.2 on Linux, x86-64 and Arm64, which on an NVIDIA Jetson means JetPack 7.2 or newer. On Arm64 the first install also pulls about 2.6 GB of TensorRT libraries from NVIDIA, so give it a few minutes. It can’t reuse the TensorRT that ships with NVIDIA JetPack, because Torch-TensorRT 2.15 needs TensorRT 11.4 and JetPack 7.2 comes with TensorRT 10.

Export, in Python

import torch
import torch_tensorrt
from executorch.backends.cuda.cuda_backend import CudaBackend
from executorch.backends.cuda.cuda_partitioner import CudaPartitioner

with torch.no_grad():
    model = MyPolicy().eval().cuda()
    example = (torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224, device="cuda"),)
    exported = torch.export.export(model, example)
    trt_model = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.compile(
        exported, arg_inputs=example, min_block_size=1, truncate_double=True
    )
    torch_tensorrt.save(
        trt_model,
        "policy.pte",
        output_format="executorch",
        # Everything TensorRT does not take goes to the CUDA backend.
        partitioners=[CudaPartitioner([CudaBackend.generate_method_name_compile_spec("forward")])],
    )

The CUDA backend needs a CUDA toolkit (nvcc) at export time, and it writes aoti_cuda_blob.ptd next to the .pte. Give each export its own folder and ship both files. If your model has several parts, say a vision encoder and an action head, you can put them all in one program, one method per part, with torch_tensorrt.executorch.export(). It gives you back a program you can still edit before saving.

Run, in Python, without torch

In ExecuTorch 1.6 the Python runtime no longer needs the torch library. NumPy arrays in, NumPy arrays out:

import numpy as np
import torch_tensorrt_executorch_runtime  # registers the TensorRT backend
from executorch.runtime import Runtime

program = Runtime.get().load_program("policy.pte", data_path="aoti_cuda_blob.ptd")
policy = program.load_method("forward")
actions = np.asarray(policy.execute([np.zeros((1, 3, 224, 224), np.float32)])[0])

This matters on a small board. On the Orin Nano, just importing PyTorch takes about 2.2 s and 550 MB. For a robot that only runs models, this installs just the runtime, the TensorRT backend, and the TensorRT and CUDA libraries they need, about 4.6 GB instead of 11 GB for the full install:

pip install --no-deps executorch==1.6.0 torch-tensorrt-executorch-runtime==0.2.1 \
  nvidia-cuda-runtime==13.2.86 tensorrt-cu13-libs==11.4.0.106 numpy

Run, in C++

#include <executorch/extension/module/module.h>
#include <executorch/extension/tensor/tensor.h>

using namespace executorch::aten;
using namespace executorch::extension;

Module policy("policy.pte", "aoti_cuda_blob.ptd");
std::vector<float> pixels(1 * 3 * 224 * 224);  // filled from the camera
auto observation = make_tensor_ptr({1, 3, 224, 224}, pixels);
auto actions = policy.forward(observation);

To build the app, link the CMake packages that come with the pip install. The Torch-TensorRT ExecuTorch guide has a complete CMakeLists.txt.

If the input is already on the GPU, a camera frame for example, you can skip the copies to and from the CPU. Export with device inputs and outputs (see the CUDA backend docs) and pass the GPU pointer directly:

// A camera pipeline already wrote the image to GPU memory.
float* gpu_pixels = camera.gpu_frame();

// The policy writes its actions to GPU memory that you own.
float* gpu_actions = nullptr;
cudaMalloc(&gpu_actions, 50 * 6 * sizeof(float));  // 50 actions, 6 joints each
auto actions = from_blob(gpu_actions, {1, 50, 6}, ScalarType::Float, DeviceType::CUDA);
policy.set_output(*actions);

policy.forward(from_blob(gpu_pixels, {1, 3, 224, 224}, ScalarType::Float, DeviceType::CUDA));

Performance

We took four robot policies from LeRobot, Hugging Face’s robot-learning library: ACT, SmolVLA, pi0.5 and GR00T 1.7. Each one ran five ways on a Jetson Orin Nano Super (8 GB, about $250), with the same trained weights, the same inputs, and nothing quantized.

Time per action chunk on the Orin Nano, milliseconds, lower is better:

Policy ExecuTorch-TensorRT ONNX-TensorRT Torch-TensorRT torch.compile PyTorch eager
ACT (52M) 26 25 26 42 48
SmolVLA (450M) 120 121 120 159 765
pi0.5 (3.6B) 467 452 out of memory out of memory out of memory
GR00T 1.7 (3B, fine-tuned) 215 208 215 out of memory out of memory

Memory on the Orin Nano: what the policy’s process holds while it runs, CPU and GPU together, MiB, lower is better:

Policy ExecuTorch-TensorRT ONNX-TensorRT Torch-TensorRT torch.compile PyTorch eager
ACT 407 415 1083 1642 1435
SmolVLA 1146 1178 2615 4125 3095
pi0.5 5538 5429 out of memory out of memory out of memory
GR00T 1.7 5301 5272 6464 out of memory out of memory

Time: median of three runs of 100 chunks, after 20 warm-up chunks. Memory: median of three runs, over the last 30 s of 120 s; files the process only reads, such as the program files, are not counted, and a range means the runs differed by more than 5%. The TensorRT columns and torch.compile replay CUDA graphs. Maximum power, GPU clock locked. Bold is best in the row. Differences of a few milliseconds are within run-to-run noise. Measured with the released Torch-TensorRT 2.15.0 and ExecuTorch 1.6.0. Benchmark method and full tables.

A few things stand out:

  • On the Orin Nano, ExecuTorch-TensorRT is within 4% of ONNX-TensorRT on every policy, and up to 6.4x faster than PyTorch eager mode.
  • Memory is about the same as ONNX-TensorRT, and lower on the two small policies. The Torch-TensorRT column runs the same TensorRT engines inside PyTorch. That costs 0.7 to 1.4 GB more, and pi0.5 doesn’t fit at all.
  • pi0.5, with 3.6 billion parameters, makes a chunk of 50 actions in about half a second on the 8 GB Orin Nano, where PyTorch eager mode runs out of memory.

On an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor developer kit, the high-end robot board, resource limits are less of an issue, but memory efficiency still lets more workloads fit on the device. Again, the compiled paths end up with similar performance.

Time per action chunk on Thor, milliseconds, lower is better:

Policy ExecuTorch-TensorRT ONNX-TensorRT Torch-TensorRT torch.compile PyTorch eager
ACT 3.9 3.4 3.5 6.3 9.9
SmolVLA 29.6 29.5 29.5 39.9 165.1
pi0.5 80.5 86.1 78.2 90.6 218.9
GR00T 1.7 59.7 58.4 59.5 65.3 94.3

Memory on Thor, MiB, lower is better:

Policy ExecuTorch-TensorRT ONNX-TensorRT Torch-TensorRT torch.compile PyTorch eager
ACT 443 440 1000 2066 1793
SmolVLA 1185 1205 2701 4479 to 5203 3344 to 3568
pi0.5 5617 5495 7326 7905 7421
GR00T 1.7 5314 5261 6525 7520 7042

Same method as on the Orin Nano.

It isn’t limited to robot policies. We ran the same split on a 26-billion-parameter Gemma 4 language model with 4-bit weights on an A100. TensorRT took some parts, the CUDA backend took the rest, and the output tokens were exactly the same as with the CUDA backend alone.

Big policies on a small board

For best performance, a TensorRT engine is built for one kind of GPU, so you build it on the same kind of board it runs on. Building needs the whole model in memory, and on the 8 GB Orin Nano there isn’t room to build a 3.6-billion-parameter policy in one piece. So we split pi0.5 and GR00T into a chain of smaller programs. Each one is built in its own process from only its own weights, so the full checkpoint is never in memory at once. Both policies make actions by repeating one “denoising” step, so that step is a single program that runs ten times for pi0.5 and four times for GR00T. The programs hand tensors to each other on the GPU.

At run time the TensorRT backend loads its engines through ExecuTorch’s shared GPU memory allocator, so there are no extra copies. Without it, pi0.5’s second engine wouldn’t load on the Orin Nano at all. Engines can also be larger than 2 GB and can live in a .ptd file next to the .pte, like other large data in ExecuTorch. On discrete GPUs, weight streaming also runs engines that don’t fit in GPU memory.

Several policies on one GPU

A robot rarely runs just one model. A big policy plans the next moves, a perception model looks at every camera frame, and a small controller has to run at a fixed, high rate. They all share one GPU’s memory and compute.

Memory is the easier part. If one process loads the same program twice, say one policy per arm, Torch-TensorRT 2.15 keeps its engines in GPU memory only once. On the Orin Nano the second load took 76 MiB instead of 805 MiB. There’s also an option to let many engines share one working buffer per GPU.

Compute is harder. A big model can fill every streaming multiprocessor (SM), and everything else has to wait.

A CUDA green context gives a model its own fixed set of SMs. Every GPU backend in an ExecuTorch program runs on the CUDA stream you pick, so you create one stream per green context and run each policy on its own stream, in its own thread. It has to be a thread per policy, because forward() waits for its GPU work to finish:

#include <executorch/extension/cuda/caller_stream.h>

using namespace executorch::extension::cuda;

// One thread per policy. Each thread has its own green context and stream.
void run_policy(Module& policy, cudaStream_t stream) {
  CallerStreamGuard guard(stream);  // this thread's GPU work runs on this policy's SMs
  while (running) {
    policy.forward(next_input(policy));
  }
}

The helper is in executorch::extension::cuda and works with both the TensorRT and CUDA backends. A few limits:

  • Memory bandwidth and other GPU resources are still shared, so delays get shorter but don’t go away.
  • Jetsons don’t have many SMs (8 on the Orin Nano, 20 on the AGX Thor), so you can only split them a few ways.
  • Torch-TensorRT builds each engine for the whole GPU. On a green context TensorRT warns about that, and an engine that uses kernels needing more SMs than the context has can fail, so give each green context enough SMs for its engine.

What’s next

  • End-to-end compilation for big policies. NVIDIA is working on compiling big models without splitting them by hand, so a Jetson Orin Nano can build pi0.5 and GR00T as a single program, with lower latency and a simpler workflow.
  • LeRobot. We’re working with the Hugging Face LeRobot team on ExecuTorch export for LeRobot policies, so exported policies run faster than in PyTorch eager mode or torch.compile and don’t need PyTorch to run. You can follow which policies export and run on each GPU in this tracking issue, which uses newer builds than the tables above.

Learn more

  • ExecuTorch TensorRT backend docs
  • Torch-TensorRT ExecuTorch deployment guide
  • Examples in examples/torchtrt_executorch_example

What model do you want to run, on which board, and where does it break today? Tell us in an issue on Torch-TensorRT or ExecuTorch.

item.content:encoded:
The PyTorch Foundation is proud to celebrate the winners and nominees of the fourth annual PyTorch Foundation Contributor Awards!

Presented on the keynote stage at PyTorch Conference 2026 in San Jose, California, these awards recognize the individuals whose dedication, innovation, and contributions help advance open source projects and strengthen the communities around them.

2026 Awards at a Glance

15 Award Winners | 11 Nominees | 9 Award Categories | 3 New Categories

This year marks another milestone for the program, with 15 award winners, up from 11 in 2025, recognizing outstanding contributions across PyTorch Foundation-hosted projects, including PyTorch, vLLM, Ray, and DeepSpeed.

Expanding Recognition Across the PyTorch Ecosystem

As the PyTorch Foundation’s community continues to grow, the Contributor Awards have evolved to reflect the diverse ways individuals contribute to its projects.

In 2026, three new award categories were introduced:

  • Knowledge Enhancer: Celebrating contributors who make knowledge more accessible through documentation, tutorials, and educational resources.
  • Bug Buster: Recognizing those who identify, report, and resolve bugs that improve project quality and reliability.
  • Catalyst: Honoring contributions that improve developer workflows, automation, infrastructure, and AI-supported development.

These additions complement the existing categories recognizing technical innovation, mentorship, community leadership, and ecosystem development.

Meet the 2026 Contributor Award Winners

Congratulations to our 15 award winners across nine categories!

Superhero

  • Thomas Ortner — PyTorch

Ecosystem Champion

  • Guangye Yu — PyTorch

Knowledge Enhancer

  • Abdulsalam Yazid Bande — PyTorch
  • Suman Debnath — Ray

  • Guilherme Vieira Leobas — PyTorch
  • Vishal Goyal — PyTorch

Newcomer

  • Johannes Lennart Zeiser — PyTorch
  • Jiangyun Zhu — vLLM

Review Powerhouse

  • Wentao Ye — vLLM

Innovator

  • Elfie Guo — PyTorch
  • Masahiro Tanaka — DeepSpeed
  • Xinan Lin — PyTorch

Catalyst

  • Harry Mellor — vLLM
  • Jiahao Tan — PyTorch

Outstanding Ambassador

  • Jiho Kim — PyTorch

Recognizing Our 2026 Award Nominees

We also celebrate the 11 award nominees whose contributions and dedication continue to make a difference across the PyTorch ecosystem.

  • Chandra Mohan Singh Negi
  • Arun Bhandari
  • Masahiro Hiramori
  • Luka Govedič
  • Irakli Salia
  • Jiahao Chen
  • Kunshang Ji
  • Rohit Kumar Tiwari
  • Subin George
  • Aaron Gokaslan
  • Xunzhuo Liu

Congratulations to all our winners and nominees! Your work helps make the PyTorch ecosystem stronger, more collaborative, and more accessible to developers around the world.

Explore the 2026 Contributor Awards and view the honorees

Award Ceremony

Watch the award ceremony at PyTorch Conference North America. 

Thank You to Our Community and Sponsor

A special thank you to the Contributor Awards Program Committee for the time, care, and thoughtful consideration invested in reviewing nominations and supporting this year’s awards.

We also extend our appreciation to Red Hat, sponsor of the 2026 PyTorch Foundation Contributor Awards, for supporting this important community recognition program.

And most importantly, thank you to the contributors who continue to build, maintain, document, improve, and champion projects across the PyTorch Foundation ecosystem.

item.dc:creator: PyTorch Foundation

item.content:encoded:
PyTorch Foundation Ambassadors bring people together to learn, share technical knowledge and contribute to PyTorch Foundation projects and the wider open-source AI ecosystem.

In this November roundup, we highlight some of our ambassadors’ activities, including local meetups, university sessions, technical articles and practical learning resources.

PyTorch Community Meetup in Kampala

On September 19, Pacifique Mugisho organized an in-person PyTorch East Africa community meetup at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, in collaboration with the IndabaX Makerere Student Chapter and the IEEE Computer Society Makerere Student Branch.

The event received 103 registrations and welcomed 32 attendees. Talks explored retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), external knowledge integration and advanced retrieval techniques. Pacifique also led a practical workshop covering embeddings, semantic search and how these components can be combined in PyTorch-based applications.

An interactive quiz gave participants another way to engage with the material. Following the event, the community gained 20 WhatsApp members and four LinkedIn members. The gathering also laid the groundwork for further in-person meetups.

Technical talks and hands-on learning at the PyTorch East Africa community meetup at Makerere University, Kampala.

Hands-on PyTorch on TPUs in Dhaka

On October 30, Zaynul Abedin Miah delivered a technical talk and live demonstration, “PyTorch on TPU with TorchTPU,” at a community meetup in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

The session showed students and early-career developers how to run native PyTorch on Google TPUs using free Colab notebooks. It covered device setup, tensor operations and torch.compile, with an interactive “predict, then run” exercise.

The event received 91 registrations, and all 50 approved seats were filled. Participants travelled from several cities, with some journeys exceeding 330 kilometres. Slides and a runnable notebook were shared with all registrants so they could continue experimenting afterward.

View the event. Colab: Link

Attendees and a live demonstration at the PyTorch on TPUs community session in Dhaka.

Efficient LLM Inference with PyTorch Community Nepal

On November 1, Arun Bhandari organized and hosted PyTorch Community Nepal’s first online technical session, “Accelerating LLM Inference with Speculative Decoding at the Edge.”

Guest speaker Manjil Nepal, a Research Associate at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, discussed speculative decoding in edge–server environments and approaches to improving draft models through local and federated learning.

Arun coordinated the speaker, registration, promotion, moderation and audience discussion. The session attracted 86 registrations and 20 attendees, with presentation slides and source code shared afterward.

The event created an opportunity for researchers and Nepal’s AI and machine learning community to exchange knowledge and connect through a technical discussion.

PyTorch Community Nepal’s online session on efficient LLM inference.

AI Research with PyTorch in Nigeria

During September, Abdulsalam Yazid Bande delivered two introductory sessions for academic audiences in Nigeria, reaching 75 attendees.

“From Research Question to PyTorch Experiment” introduced 35 graduate and postgraduate students to modern AI, neural networks, generative AI and PyTorch’s role in research.

A second session, “Getting Started with AI Research Using PyTorch,” welcomed 40 faculty members for a practical introduction to experimentation, model development and machine learning applications in academic research.

Together, the sessions helped students and faculty explore how PyTorch could support their own research questions.

Introducing AI research with PyTorch to academic audiences in Nigeria.

LLM Application Development at Vilnius Tech

In September, Eyup Cinar visited Vilnius Tech University in Lithuania to deliver a guest lecture on rapid application development with large language models.

Approximately 30 undergraduate and graduate students attended. The session introduced the PyTorch ecosystem and its role in developing, training and deploying LLM-based applications, while providing an opportunity for academic exchange between institutions.

A guest lecture on LLM application development at Vilnius Tech.

Getting Started with Open Source at Duke University

On September 4, Sahdev Zala presented to more than 25 students in Duke University’s AI Engineering master’s program in Durham, North Carolina.

The session helped students understand how to get started contributing to PyTorch and Kubernetes. Participants joined both in person and online to explore opportunities to contribute to open-source projects.

Exploring open-source contributions with Duke University students.

LLM Post-Training at DevFest Kuala Lumpur

On November 14, Vensen Mu, PyTorch Foundation Ambassador and RL-Kernel maintainer, delivered “Practical Train–Inference Consistency in LLM RL Post-Training” at Google DevFest Kuala Lumpur 2026.

The talk explored numerical discrepancies between training and inference systems in reinforcement learning for large language models. Vensen shared how the open-source RL-Kernel project works toward bitwise consistency across training and rollout workflows, including engineering considerations relevant to PyTorch and vLLM.

The session encouraged developers interested in AI infrastructure and reliable RL post-training to explore the problem and collaborate through open source.

Read the event announcement and explore RL-Kernel.

Sharing PyTorch Updates in Simplified Chinese

Zhiqing Xiao published a Simplified Chinese WeChat article introducing PyTorch 2.14.

The article received more than 300 views, helping Chinese-speaking readers learn about the release.

Read the article in Simplified Chinese.

Transfer Learning: Articles, Code and Community Talks

Sahdev Zala published an IBM Developer article based on a transfer-learning demonstration using PyTorch and Torchvision’s pretrained ResNet-18 model. He also made the accompanying source code publicly available, giving readers an example to explore and build on.

Read the transfer-learning article and explore the accompanying code.

Thank You to Our Ambassadors

Thank you to our ambassadors for sharing your knowledge, creating learning opportunities and bringing people together around PyTorch.

item.title: Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels
item.dc:creator: Caleb Min Sup Kim, Ethan Che, Jongsok Choi, Jason Ansel
item.description:
TL;DR Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and...

The post Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and chooses block sizes, warps, and stages, giving near-autotuned speed for free.

Introduction

Helion, PyTorch’s domain-specific language (DSL) for performance portable machine learning kernels, relies heavily on autotuning for its performance. Autotuning time can be a major bottleneck: for example, a previous team tuning a single paged-attention kernel across 72 shapes spent 10 hours in Helion’s quick mode, and 25 at full effort. To address these issues, we’ve developed a set of heuristics that read a kernel’s IR and dataflow at compile time and emit a config directly, without any autotuning.

We classify kernels into broad families based on the operations they contain – matmul, reduction, or pointwise – and apply a family-specific heuristic to each. These families are intentionally general: the matmul heuristic, for example, looks for any kernel containing a matmul operation such as hl.dot or torch.baddbmm, not just standard m-n-k matrix multiplications. These are designed to be generic and apply broadly to custom kernels that users may write.

Highlights:

  • Autotuner Heuristics. Our heuristics cover a large set of kernels, including GEMM, reductions, and even linear attention.
  • Linear attention. Over 96 kernel-and-shape cells spanning nine linear-attention variants, the computed config beats the hand-written Triton in Flash Linear Attention (FLA) by 1.18x in the forward pass, and by 1.12x with backward included on H100. Overall the heuristic is 2.13x faster than Helion’s previous no-autotune default on H100.
  • vLLM reduction kernels. Over 153 kernel-and-shape cells across six production kernels on H100, the computed config is 1.27x faster than vLLM’s own handwritten CUDA/C++ operators, and 2.2x faster than Helion’s previous default.
  • The analysis itself is cheap. Compiling a kernel with the heuristics on versus off differs negligibly (tens of milliseconds), which is lost in the noise of Triton compilation.

Our Approach: Decide the Config at Compile Time

A single Helion kernel can lower into thousands of different Triton kernels. One definition covers block sizes, loop orders, indexing modes and pipelining strategies, but the autotuner has to choose which of those thousands to emit, by compiling and benchmarking many candidates. And this autotuning cost is per kernel and per shape, which multiplies the problem the more kernels, shapes, and hardware backends you want to support.

We compute the config at compile time instead of searching for it at tuning time. We read the device IR and record structural facts about it: which axes are tiled, which block sizes are tunable, which tiles are live at which part of the kernel, etc. A heuristic reads those facts and emits a config.

The point here is not to come up with a better config than the autotuner, which has the benefit of benchmarking potentially thousands of configs before selecting one. It is to add a point in the tradeoff space between performance and wait time.

Our heuristics serve two purposes. A primary heuristic emits the default config used when autotuning is disabled. When autotuning is enabled, helper heuristics generate roughly 5–20 related or alternative configs that seed the autotuner. The goals are different: the default config should perform well on its own, while the seeds should give the autotuner several promising starting points to speed up autotuning. In this blog, we’ll touch on both, but focus on the primary heuristic that gets emitted with autotuning off.

How the Heuristics Work

A heuristic sets the values for various config knobs, which must be tuned carefully to achieve high performance and are normally picked by the autotuner. These include block sizes for each tiled axis, num_warps, num_stages, the L2 grouping, load eviction policies, and more.

We pick a heuristic by scanning the device IR for the operations a kernel contains. Any matmul routes to the matmul heuristic regardless of what else is in the kernel; a reduction with no matmul routes to the reduction heuristic; everything else receives the pointwise heuristic. If a kernel’s extents are not all known at compile time, no heuristic fires and Helion falls back to the original default.

Our heuristics all lean on the same underlying analysis, which estimates resource usage of the kernel. At any step of the kernel, the analysis determines: given a candidate set of block sizes, how many registers, shared memory, and — on Blackwell — how much tensor memory, one CTA needs at that moment.

To do this, we run a liveness analysis on the compiler IR and walk each graph to find where every value is last used, and guess where it will be placed in memory. This is a hard problem: we are trying to predict what Triton will keep in registers, what it will stage through shared memory, what it will materialize at all rather than fuse away. Sometimes it is easier to predict (e.g., we assume the output of an hl.dot will be placed in TMEM on B200), but the estimate is approximate.

Using this we can estimate things that matter for performance, such as:

  • Occupancy: how many CTAs fit on an SM at once. Whichever space runs out first decides it, e.g., a CTA needing a tenth of the SM’s registers and a tenth of its shared memory, but six tenths of its tensor memory, gets one CTA per SM, since two CTAs would go over the tensor memory budget by 20% (0.6 x 2 = 1.2).
  • Register pressure: Peak live registers spread over the threads we intend to launch tells us whether the assembler will be forced to spill.

These considerations inform the selection of different config knobs. We’ll illustrate this for the matmul heuristic:

  • block_size: If the launch produces fewer CTAs than the GPU has SMs, we shrink block size on a grid axis to produce more of them.
  • num_stages: More stages hide more load latency, so we want as many as shared memory allows. But stages can also accidentally lose occupancy: six of them might fit while eating the CTA’s entire shared-memory budget, leaving one CTA per SM, where three stages and two CTAs per SM is the better trade.
  • num_warps. Two things pull on this:
    • Which instruction Triton emits. Below four warps, or with an M block under 64, Triton uses the smaller synchronous MMA; otherwise it uses the big high-throughput one (wgmma on Hopper, tcgen05 on Blackwell). Usually we want the big one. But when there is little matmul work sometimes the better answer is many CTAs per SM running small MMAs that overlap each other’s loads. So we count dynamic matmul work (essentially counting the number of times the hl.dot will be executed dynamically) and choose based on that.
    • Register pressure. Warps divide the tile across more threads, so more warps means less pressure on each one. If the peak live state at the current count would spill, that argues for increasing warps.
  • Feasibility Check. A final pessimistic pass over the whole kernel: add up tensor memory, shared memory and registers, and confirm the config can actually launch. The adjustments above already respect these budgets, so this is mostly defensive.

In the case where there are multiple matmuls in one kernel (for example for attention and linear attention), we run the matmul heuristic on each hl.dot and use those as the starting point. They may disagree: two dots can share one block-size knob — one dot’s N is frequently the next dot’s K — and there is only one num_warps for the whole kernel.

To resolve these tradeoffs, we rank each dot by estimated importance: priority goes to any dot with a loop-carried accumulator, since that accumulator stays resident for the whole loop and its tile sets the kernel’s footprint; then its dynamic matmul work; then its own output area. Wherever two dots disagree about a knob, the higher-ranked one wins (for example num_warps is set by the top-ranked dot alone).

The reduction heuristic works through a similar set of knobs:

  • num_warps. Three pressures here, pulling in different directions:
    • Enough warps to do the reduction. A wide reduction needs warps working on it, so a ladder off the largest selected reduction sets the starting point: 128 elements wants one or two warps, 16,384 wants many more.
    • Residency. More warps per CTA means fewer CTAs per SM (there is a per-SM CTA limit), so we also test fewer warps.
    • Register pressure. Adjust warps to not spill registers.
  • block_size. Fitting more CTAs per SM means potentially smaller tiles, so we shrink blocks back down to buy residency. The constraint is that an axis with stride 1 is the one carrying the coalesced loads, and shrinking it too far loses load coalescing.
  • Persistence. A reduction can be kept resident and done in one pass, or walked in chunks. The case that matters is a row the kernel reads twice — RMSNorm reads it once to compute the scale and again to apply it — and when we can prove that, staying persistent is allowed to cost some spilling and some residency, because it saves the second trip to memory.

Because the warp count depends on the blocks and the blocks depend on the warp count, we iterate until both hold still for a full round (in practice this doesn’t take very long).

Result 1: Config Quality, with No Tuning Time

Linear attention

We measured nine linear-attention variants in forward and forward-plus-backward, over six production shapes, on H100. The six shapes span batch 1 to 8, 8 to 96 heads, sequence 1024 to 16384 and head dimension 64 to 256. The baseline is Flash Linear Attention (FLA), an open-source, widely used library of hand-written Triton kernels. The autotuned arm in the charts (“Helion AOT config”) is the result of running the full autotuner once per shape and saving the winner — how you would ship a Helion kernel for a known set of shapes today.

Before this work the choice was binary: take Helion’s no-autotune default and run at 0.52x of handwritten FLA Triton, or spend GPU-hours autotuning and reach 1.26x. The heuristic adds a third option that did not exist before: 1.18x, with no autotuning price (most of what autotuning finds, available immediately) and it moves Helion’s out-of-the-box behavior from losing to handwritten Triton to beating it, at least for this set of kernels.

vLLM’s reduction kernels

vLLM is a widely deployed open-source LLM inference engine, and it ships its own hand-written CUDA/C++ kernels for the operations on its serving hot path. There are six reduction kernels — two FP8 quantizers, RMSNorm and SiLU-and-multiply each fused with quantization, and fused QK-normalization plus RoPE– for which vLLM already had Helion implementations, contributed by the team behind an earlier post in this series. That makes them a good test: production kernels, written by someone else, against the hand-written CUDA they were meant to replace.

And we get a similar result, in a different codebase. Helion’s no-autotune default runs at 0.58x of vLLM’s CUDA; the computed config reaches 1.27x; full autotuning gets to 1.31x. The interesting number is the last gap: on these kernels autotuning buys only about 3% over the config we compute for free.

The everyday kernels, against torch.compile

Both comparisons above are specialist libraries — linear-attention variants and FP8 quantizers. This one is deliberately the opposite: the kernels everybody writes. RMSNorm, LayerNorm, softmax, cross entropy and friends, similar to the suite the introduction post benchmarked when it first measured Helion. Most of the kernels benchmarked in this section can be found here.

The reference baseline here is torch.compile(mode=”max-autotune-no-cudagraphs”): we force torch.compile onto its Triton backend so we are not comparing against handwritten libraries (e.g.. cuBLAS) but instead against generated Triton from a widely-used compiler. There is no tuned-config arm in this section, for the mundane reason that we do not have full autotune runs for these kernels (which would take many GPU hours to produce).

On a suite of ten reduction kernels and 80 (kernel, shape) combinations, the computed config comes out at 1.09x of max-autotune torch.compile, with no tuning of its own. Helion’s unseeded default is 0.27x.

We also sweep across thirteen matmul kernel families over 70 shapes. The computed config comes out at 1.88x of max-autotune torch.compile overall, against 0.51x for Helion’s default. Two caveats on that 1.88x. The comparisons are not always apples-to-apples – for some of these kernels the PyTorch implementation materializes intermediates that the Helion kernel fuses. And jagged HSTU attention is a genuine regression: the old default happens to land on a good config there (3.72x) and the heuristic does worse (3.27x).

Result 2: Does the Seed Make the Search Faster?

Everything above is about the config Helion emits when autotuning is off. But the same configs can be handed to the autotuner as its starting population, and in principle a good starting point should let the search finish sooner. In addition to this primary config, the helper heuristics also add somewhere between 5 and 20 new variations / approaches.

To test it we took 38 matmul and multi-matmul kernels — linear attention, attention, Mamba, and other wild cards like squeeze-and-excitation — and one shape for each kernel. Then we ran the full autotune effort on every cell twice: once from random configs, once with the compiler’s seeds in the initial population.

The short answer from this run is that seeding buys a lot early but much less late. Here is one cell, chosen as a clear example of the pattern. The x-axis tracks the number of configs tried, while the y-axis tracks performance relative to the best config we found.

Seeded, the first config is far superior to the unseeded first config. But unseeded quickly catches up, and they end up sitting on the same answer while the search grinds through several hundred more configs. The early advantage is enormous while the final advantage is zero.

That is the pattern across all 38 cells. Medians below; counts include configs that failed to compile or failed to produce a timing, since those consume budget too.

Search target Median configs (no seeds / seeded)
within 50% of the best found 35.5 / 1.0
within 25% 103.5 / 2.5
within 5% 255.5 / 175.0
complete search 521.5 / 420.5

The advantage is concentrated entirely at the start: 35x fewer configs to reach something merely decent, 41x to get within 25%, but only 1.5x to get within 5% and 1.2x to finish the search.

One thing this result is not: seeding does not make the final config any better. Replaying both arms’ winners on one GPU, they land within a fraction of a percent of each other. This is about how long the search takes, not where it ends up.

Limitations and Future Work

A central limitation is that these heuristics predict what another compiler will do. Every budget depends on guessing where a value ends up — registers, shared memory, or tensor memory — and that is Triton’s decision, not ours. Some of it is safe to bet on: on B200 a matmul result is going to be in tensor memory. Plenty of it we get wrong. There are several possible directions of future work.

Measure instead of predicting. The cleanest fix for the limitation above is to stop guessing: compile once, read the register and shared-memory usage the assembler reported, and correct the estimate from there.

Fire on more kernels. We currently decline whenever we lack the information to size anything — a loop tiled over a range only known at runtime, for instance. A less-educated guess would be easy: a default extent, a mean, something. Configs would be worse without that information, but the alternative today is the base default, which the results above show is very bad — so the guess is probably still worth making.

Touch more knobs. We set block sizes, num_warps and num_stages, plus some L2 grouping and L2 eviction policy. That leaves a long list untouched — tensor descriptors versus pointer arithmetic, persistent versus flat launch, etc. Individually these are probably worth less than the ones we do set, but there is certainly performance left on the table.

Specialize the heuristics. They are deliberately general: one multi-matmul heuristic has to do well on attention and linear attention, one reduction heuristic on RMSNorm and vLLM’s quantization kernels. An alternative is parent heuristics with children — a vLLMQuantizationHeuristic that starts from ReductionHeuristic’s answer and then specializes on what it knows about that family.

Other backends. Everything here is evaluated on NVIDIA, and the heuristics ship enabled for H100 and B200 on the Triton backend. Nothing in the approach is NVIDIA-specific — the analysis is parameterized by hardware limits that should apply across backends — but the constants and ladders were tuned against these two chips.

Conclusion

These heuristics are merged into Helion and enabled by default on H100 and B200 with the Triton backend. If you would like to learn more, please check out the autotuner heuristics.

The point is not that static analysis beats search, but rather that the gap is now small enough that skipping the search is a reasonable thing to do for some kernels. Helion’s out-of-the-box behavior went from 0.52x handwritten FLA Triton to 1.18x, and from 0.58x vLLM’s handwritten CUDA to 1.27x, with nothing compiled and nothing benchmarked. On a general suite of reduction kernels it sits at 1.09x torch.compile max-autotune. Full autotuning remains the right call when you are shipping a fixed set of shapes and can pay for it once; what changed is that the alternative is no longer a large concession.

The post Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels appeared first on PyTorch.

item.title: Integrating SGLang into Spyre in Under a Week with AI
item.dc:creator: Gal Bloch (IBM), Itay Etelis (IBM), Raghu Ganti (IBM), Mudhakar Srivatsa (IBM), Alex Nails (RadixArk)
item.description:
TL;DR With help from AI coding agents, our two-person team integrated SGLang with IBM Spyre in less than a week, building a plugin of roughly 1,500 lines. Existing Spyre support...

The post Integrating SGLang into Spyre in Under a Week with AI appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

With help from AI coding agents, our two-person team integrated SGLang with IBM Spyre in less than a week, building a plugin of roughly 1,500 lines. Existing Spyre support in PyTorch and SGLang’s clear extension points made it straightforward to reuse the hardware code. SGLang delivered about 3.6× the throughput of the reference PyTorch inference implementation using torch-spyre. It was also on par with vLLM on the workloads measured for Granite 3.3 8B and Gemma 4 26B A4B. Prefix sharing through RadixCache worked without any Spyre-specific changes.

We work on IBM’s Spyre accelerator and wanted to make SGLang‘s serving stack, including its built-in prefix sharing, available to Spyre users.

In less than a week, the two of us used AI-assisted development to integrate SGLang into IBM Spyre with a plugin of just ~1,500 lines of code. A key factor was building on existing PyTorch hardware support and SGLang’s well-defined extension points. This allowed the two of us, alongside our AI coding agents, to integrate a new accelerator into SGLang in a remarkably short time. The AI coding agents used existing PyTorch implementations of Spyre operations as reference code and adapted the integration code to SGLang’s backend interfaces. Their work focused on connecting the existing hardware support to the new serving framework.

Spyre and the starting point

Spyre is IBM’s accelerator for enterprise AI inference. It integrates using torch-spyre, which registers Spyre as a PyTorch device and connects it to torch.compile, exposing hardware support through standard PyTorch APIs.

The result

The initial SGLang integration took the two of us less than a week of work. The plugin was roughly 1,500 lines, building on the compiler and reusable hardware support from PyTorch. Four small patches extended SGLang’s backend support: two made existing execution paths available without CUDA-specific dependencies, and two registered Spyre as a supported device and attention backend that does not use Triton. The compatibility changes can also support other accelerators; the registration changes are specific to Spyre.

SGLang on Spyre achieved approximately 3.6× the throughput of the reference PyTorch inference implementation using torch-spyre.

We also compared SGLang and vLLM on Spyre using Granite 3.3 8B and Gemma 4 26B A4B. Across the workloads we measured for these two models, SGLang’s performance was on par with vLLM.

Relative performance of SGLang and vLLM / spyre-inference on Granite 3.3 8B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B, normalized to vLLM = 1.0. Lower is better.

Why it worked

With a working compiler and an existing inference server in place, adding SGLang became a focused integration task. PyTorch and torch.compile supplied a shared implementation layer, expressing accelerator functionality through APIs that both serving frameworks could use.

SGLang supplied clear places to connect that code. Its platform registration, attention backend, KV pool, and operator dispatch separated the integration into bounded tasks while preserving the existing scheduler, request handling, and serving loop. The reference code came from the existing vLLM integration for Spyre, including its PyTorch implementations of accelerator operations. This gave the AI coding agents concrete code for Spyre’s hardware behavior, while SGLang’s extension points defined the interfaces their adapted code had to satisfy. Together, these reduced how much the agents had to infer about the hardware and where the integration belonged.

The existing vLLM Spyre backend was about 3,500 lines, compared with roughly 1,500 for the SGLang plugin. In the initial integration, the attention base class supplied the surrounding logic, leaving the Spyre backend to override the inner scaled dot-product attention operation. Reusing that base class accounted for roughly two-thirds of the line-count difference between the two plugins. SGLang’s device-agnostic KV pool also allowed a single method override for buffer creation; allocation still needed PyTorch-based handling where the existing path relied on Triton.

Reusing the vLLM Spyre implementation

We reused the attention code from the vLLM Spyre integration, including how it groups inputs into buckets and handles tensor shapes. We also reused its PyTorch-based approach to allocating the KV cache. For RMSNorm, SiLU, GeLU, rotary embeddings, and linear layers, we connected the existing Spyre implementations to SGLang’s operator dispatch.

Some features required no Spyre-specific work at all. RadixCache is a good example: prefix sharing is resolved entirely within SGLang’s scheduler before execution reaches the accelerator, so the existing scheduling logic worked unchanged.

The plugin is available as open source alongside upstream SGLang.

Using SGLang with Spyre

The example assumes the Spyre runtime, torch-spyre, the SGLang plugin, and its compatibility patches are installed and configured.

import sglang as sgl

models = [
    "ibm-ai-platform/micro-g3.3-8b-instruct-1b",
    "mistralai/Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410",
]

for model in models:
    engine = sgl.Engine(
        model_path=model,
        device="spyre",
        attention_backend="spyre_paged",
        dtype="float16",
        page_size=64,
        max_running_requests=1,
        disable_cuda_graph=True,
    )

    try:
        output = engine.generate(
            "Why is the sky blue?",
            {"temperature": 0, "max_new_tokens": 64},
        )
        print(model, output["text"])
    finally:
        engine.shutdown()

Looking ahead

The Spyre software stack continues to evolve rapidly.

Over the coming months, we expect to add support for dynamic shapes, reducing much of the shape management required today. Later this year, we also expect to bring Triton support to Spyre and enable RadixAttention on top of it, opening the door to additional kernel optimizations.

Keeping hardware support in PyTorch and integration code at SGLang’s extension points gives future compiler and runtime improvements a path into the serving stack. The next integration can start from the same shared foundation, with concrete implementations and interfaces that developers and AI coding tools can work with.

The post Integrating SGLang into Spyre in Under a Week with AI appeared first on PyTorch.

item.title: Training a 1T-Parameter MoE on EU public infrastructure with PyTorch and TorchTitan
item.dc:creator: The EUROPA consortium (Domyn, Fraunhofer IAIS and IIS)
item.description:
TL;DR Scaling pretraining for a ~1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on shared, public infrastructure was previously considered unfeasible due to unique architectural and interconnect bottlenecks. However, by leveraging the fine-grained flexibility...

The post Training a 1T-Parameter MoE on EU public infrastructure with PyTorch and TorchTitan appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Scaling pretraining for a ~1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on shared, public infrastructure was previously considered unfeasible due to unique architectural and interconnect bottlenecks. However, by leveraging the fine-grained flexibility of PyTorch and TorchTitan, the EUROPA consortium successfully unlocked frontier-scale training on JUPITER, boosting throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/sec per GPU across 384 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs per DP replica (96 nodes) as part of the EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge.

The EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge was designed to prove that sovereign, open-source AI could compete at frontier levels using shared public resources. As part of that process, we – as the EUROPA consortium, formed by Domyn and Fraunhofer IAIS and IIS – were selected to an open European Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model of at least 400B parameters, support for all 24 official EU languages, and strict compliance with the EU AI Act.

In this post, we describe how we scaled pretraining to 1T MoE on JUPITER, the EuroHPC exascale supercomputer hosted at Forschungszentrum Jülich, proving that public infrastructure can indeed sustain frontier scale.

Total parameters 951.9B (32.8B active per token)
Layers 74
Hidden size 6,144
Experts 384 routed, top-8
Expert hidden size 1,792
Vocabulary 256,000
Pretrain Sequence length 65,536 tokens
Optimizer Muon + AdamW

The table lists the configuration used for the experiments in the post.

Models of this size are usually trained on clusters that their developers operate or rent for exclusive use. JUPITER is instead publicly funded research infrastructure shared by hundreds of projects. It was also designed to support scientific research at large, which led to architectural choices that are somewhat atypical in the AI space, as we’ll describe in detail later in the post. As such, reaching the 1T parameter scale while maintaining viable throughput requires careful optimizations that go beyond standard distributed techniques.

In order to have access to the necessary level of flexibility to perform fine-grained optimizations to the pre-training setup, we chose to go with PyTorch and TorchTitan. Under these conditions, we raised throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200 GPUs (96 nodes). We want to share the main milestones that get us there, each of which builds on TorchTitan’s design and led to contributions back to TorchTitan and PyTorch:

  1. FlexShard placement for the Muon optimizer, which removes most of the optimizer’s communication.
  2. Activation-checkpoint offloading to the Grace CPU.
  3. Running FSDP’s all-gather setup on the compute stream (unshard_async_op), which frees ~14 GiB of HBM per GPU.

The full write-up covers the remaining changes in detail, with interactive figures and profiler traces.

The machine and its constraints

Each JUPITER Booster node has four NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. Each superchip pairs a Hopper GPU (96 GB HBM3) with a 72-core Grace CPU (120 GB LPDDR5X), connected by a 900 GB/s NVLink-C2C link. GPUs in a node are connected by NVLink 4 at 150 GB/s per direction, and each node has four InfiniBand NDR200 adapters, about 25 GB/s per GPU.

Figure 2. Bandwidths within a JUPITER node, drawn to scale. All inter-node traffic leaves through the thin InfiniBand links.

In addition to the accelerators, two key parts of the system are also relevant for the design:

  • Inter-node bandwidth. InfiniBand is 36 times slower than the link between a GPU and its own CPU, and distributing a 1T parameter model over hundreds of accelerators requires crossing that boundary continuously during training. Traffic over InfiniBand must therefore aggressively overlap with computation.
  • Host memory capacity. GH200 is available with up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X per Grace, but JUPITER’s compute nodes actually use the 120 GB configuration (as opposed to login nodes which sport 480GB), which favors bandwidth over capacity. After the kernel’s share, about 108 GiB per GPU is usable, and we found that in practice some nodes start jobs with much less. This limits how much state can be moved out of the HBM.

These constraints dictate the parallelism layout: 384-way FSDP with 4-way expert parallelism inside each node and no pipeline parallelism. The MoE token all-to-all is hard to overlap, so we kept it on NVLink. Without pipeline parallelism steps tend to be shorter, which has the advantage of providing fast feedback at scale, and fixed costs are amortized via a large batch of 384 sequences of 65,536 tokens (~25M tokens per step). FSDP already provides us with the overlap of the gather of layer n+1 with the compute of layer n, so most of the remaining work goes into making the overlap effective. We achieve this across three dimensions: moving to longer sequences to compute for longer, reducing the bytes transmitted over InfiniBand, and leveraging Grace memory to provide enough total capacity to hold the model, the gradients and the optimizer state.

FlexShard: Muon without the communication

We use Muon for every weight matrix except the router and embeddings (about 99.5% of the parameters) and AdamW for the rest. Muon requires one fp32 state per parameter, while Adam requires two. Removing the second state is instrumental in making a 65,536-token sequence fit in memory.

Muon orthogonalizes each update with a few Newton-Schulz iterations, which operate on the whole matrix. Because FSDP splits every matrix into 384 shards, a simple implementation gathers each matrix on one rank, runs Newton-Schulz there and scatters the result back. On our interconnect, this communication is too expensive.

FlexShard, now part of TorchTitan, lets us control which rank owns which parameters. We shard the experts by whole expert, so every rank owns complete expert matrices and runs their Newton-Schulz iterations with no communication at all. The dense matrices, such as the attention projections, are still collected on an owning rank, and each rank processes its own experts while the dense matrices are in transit, so that communication is overlapped.

With FSDP’s CPU offload, the optimizer runs on Grace, where the parameters are stored, and Newton-Schulz on 72 Arm cores takes ~35 s per step. We contributed support to TorchTitan for running Newton-Schulz on the GPU while parameters stay offloaded. The optimizer step went from 41.7 s to 2.2 s, and throughput rose from 441 to 597 tokens/s per GPU (+35%).

Figure 3. Rank 0’s profiled step from 80 s onward. Top: Newton-Schulz on Grace, with the GPU idle for ~34 s after the backward pass while the CPU computes. Bottom: Newton-Schulz on Hopper, where the optimizer takes a small fraction of the step.

Activation offloading to Grace

The volume of weights gathered per layer does not depend on the number of tokens in our setup, so a longer sequence increases compute time while not impacting communication. We first stored activations only at layer boundaries and recomputed everything inside a layer during the backward pass. In TorchTitan this is named FullAC. Since GPU was idle for most of the baseline step, the extra compute did not lengthen it. As a result, throughput went from 90 to 370 tokens/s per GPU at 32,768 tokens.

At 65,536 tokens, the boundary activations alone take 74 layers × 65,536 tokens × 6,144 × 2 bytes ≈ 55 GiB per GPU, which does not fit in HBM next to the weights. GH200 has a 900 GB/s link to 120 GB of CPU memory, so we decide to offload them. Each boundary activation is copied to Grace after the forward pass produces it, and copied back to Hopper one layer before the backward pass recomputes it. An offloading parameter sets the share of layers that offload, which trades HBM for Grace memory.

TorchTitan’s activation-checkpointing wrapper made this change convenient. We contributed the hooks for activation-checkpoint offloading to TorchTitan and built our offloading strategy on top of them. With offload, throughput rose from 370 to 508 tokens/s per GPU (+37%), and the sequence length grew to 49,152 tokens and then, with Muon, to 65,536.

Figure 4. Offload schedule, drawn with 16 layers in place of 74. During the forward pass, each boundary activation moves to Grace. During the backward pass, it returns to HBM one layer before its recomputation.

De-fragging FSDPs Streams

After an upgrade to our software stack, the CUDA caching allocator started retrying allocations on every rank at ~70% memory utilization. At the time of the retries, 25-30 GiB of HBM was free, but the allocator could not use it.

After investigating the root cause, we identified it in how FSDP overlaps communication with computation. FSDP uses one compute stream and four side streams, and the allocator keeps a separate pool per stream. Memory freed by a stream can only be reused by that stream. FSDP allocates each buffer on the stream that writes it, and some of our other communication optimizations allocated temporary buffers inside FSDP’s calls, so these buffers also landed on side streams. Replaying the allocator’s event log at peak memory showed the side streams holding 27.3 GiB, of which only 6.4 GiB was in use. The remaining 20.9 GiB was out of reach of the compute stream, which then could not find a 4 GiB block for a MoE buffer.

Figure 5. HBM held by each allocator stream’s cache at peak live memory, reconstructed from the allocator’s event trace on rank 0. Solid bars are live tensors, and dashed bars are cached memory that only the owning stream can reuse.

Luckily, FSDP2 has a private flag, unshard_async_op, that runs the all-gather setup on the compute stream and lets NCCL run on its internal stream. The gather buffers are then allocated from, and returned to, the compute stream’s pool. We adapted our custom gather to run asynchronously, so the compute stream waits for the network only when it needs the weights. This brought the number of ranks with allocator retries from 384 to zero. Peak reserved memory went from 88.1 to 74.6 GiB, and throughput rose from 996 to 1,210 tokens/s per GPU.

We proposed a TorchTitan option to enable the flag. Following the review, unshard_async_op is being moved into a public FSDP API (PyTorch #202343), so other FSDP users can rely on it.

Upstreaming contributions and closing remarks

The configuration we just described allows to scale pre-training runs to 1T parameters at a workable throughput on public European infrastructure. In order to make it possible for others to reproduce these results (more details are available in a companion post), we upstreamed all the fixes to PyTorch and TorchTitan.

In addition to the three contributions we already mentioned, we contributed a shared RoPE cache to TorchTitan (2.56 GiB per GPU at our sequence length), skipping the embedding re-gather in the backward pass, and configurable seed-offset mesh axes. In PyTorch, we fixed CPU initialization resetting the RNG state and trunc_normal_ all-gathering DTensors. We also reported unattributed host memory at job start to the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, since it affects every user of the machine.

Thanks to the level of control provided by PyTorch and TorchTitan, training now runs at a sustained throughput of ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200s per DDP replica, for a total of 1536 GPUs for 4 DDP replicas, and fits in memory by fully leveraging the HBM and the Grace architecture. The companion post covers the rest of the path in Figure 1: data and expert load balancing, reducing the bytes sent over InfiniBand, node-local resharding, dynamic tile scheduling in SonicMoE and capping NCCL’s SM usage.

We are grateful to the European Commission for Frontier AI Grand Challenge award. We hope that this work will motivate further investments in public compute infrastructure and the continued growth of the European AI ecosystem.

  • Training a 1T-Parameter MoE on Jupiter (full post)
  • PyTorch
  • TorchTitan
  • FlexShard
  • Frontier AI Grand Challenge announcement
