item.title: ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser
item.dc:creator: Julian Ng-Thow-Hing, Siddartha Pothapragada, Stephen Jia, Digant Desai, Bilgin Cagatay
item.description:
TL;DR PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format. You export with torch.export to an ExecuTorch .pte file,...

The post ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  • PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format. You export with torch.export to an ExecuTorch .pte file, and the same file runs in any WebGPU browser via ExecuTorch’s new WebGPU backend.
  • It works across a broad range of models: LLMs (e.g. Llama 3.2, Qwen3, Gemma 3), vision-language (e.g. SmolVLM), segmentation, depth, object detection, super-resolution and speech-to-text (e.g. Whisper). Everything runs locally in the tab, and no data leaves the device. Try it in the ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground.
  • On the same machine, WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch’s CPU path (Webassembly + XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode.

Why the Browser?

The web is the largest deployment surface with billions of users on Chrome, Firefox and Safari. Browser inference ensures privacy by keeping users’ prompts, model inputs, and outputs on the user’s device rather than the server. This reduces network latency, enables offline use-cases, and lowers server-side inference costs. With the ExecuTorch WebGPU backend, PyTorch models get a native path to GPU-accelerated inference in WebGPU-enabled browsers on desktop, laptop and mobile.

WebGPU, the modern successor to WebGL, provides native compute shaders, shared memory, storage buffers, and barriers, making it viable for high-performance ML inference directly in the browser. Today, running a PyTorch model in the browser usually means first converting it to another framework’s format, such as GGUF, ONNX or TFLite. The ExecuTorch WebGPU backend lets PyTorch models reach the browser without leaving the PyTorch toolchain.

Backend Design

[Figure 1: ExecuTorch WebGPU backend design: a PyTorch model is exported once to a .pte file and runs in any WebGPU browser through the ExecuTorch Wasm runtime]

Three principles guided the WebGPU backend’s design:

  • Architecture, export, and dynamic runtime. Models export through ExecuTorch’s torch.export() and WebGPUPartitioner and run via WGSL compute shaders. At runtime, the WebGPU runtime allocates GPU buffers and dispatches compute shaders into command buffers. Dynamic shapes are handled via allocate-at-max buffers with per-dispatch workgroup recalculation to enable batched prefill, and the runtime routes shapes to specialized WGSL kernels at runtime.
  • Same artifact across multiple devices and browsers. One model (.pte file) runs in WebGPU browsers such as Chrome and Safari, natively on Metal (macOS), Vulkan (Linux/Android) and D3D12 (Windows), translating WGSL to Metal Shading Language, SPIR-V or HLSL depending on the platform. For browser deployment, the dynamic C++ runtime compiles to Webassembly via Emscripten and emdawnwebgpu bridges its WebGPU API calls to any browser’s WebGPU JavaScript API.
  • Zero friction for the end user. With WebGPU, models run in the browser sandbox with no native installation, backend server, and no data leaving the device. For developers, deployment is a .pte file served over CDN on a web page. Pipeline compilation, memory management, and dispatch scheduling are all handled through the WebGPU backend, with all data staying in GPU device memory within the browser tab.

Performance

We benchmarked ExecuTorch WebGPU against ExecuTorch’s own Webassembly (wasm) CPU backend (XNNPACK, multi-threaded) on the same machine, using quantized Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen3-0.6B in Google Chrome on Apple M1 Pro. Each data point is the median of 5 runs after 3 warmups, across 128 to 8K tokens of context, with identical token IDs for both backends. Both are timed with wall-clock time, since GPU timestamps aren’t available for CPU execution. WebGPU uses 4-bit groupwise weights (group size 64) with fp32 activations; the CPU uses XNNPACK’s 4-bit weights with 8-bit dynamic activations.

[Figure 2: ExecuTorch WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch Wasm (XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode, measured in Chrome on Apple M1 Pro]

Models in Practice

We’ve validated the WebGPU backend across models with very different architectures, demonstrating that the operator coverage generalizes beyond autoregressive text generation:

LLM Inference

  • Llama 3.2 1B (4-bit quantized)
  • Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit quantized)
  • Qwen3-0.6B (4-bit quantized)
  • Gemma 3 1B

Vision-Language Understanding

  • SmolVLM: image question answering and captioning

Vision

  • Depth Anything V2: monocular depth estimation
  • SAM 2 (SAM 2.1 Hiera Tiny): promptable image segmentation
  • D-FINE: object detection
  • Real-ESRGAN: super-resolution
  • Background Removal (MODNet): foreground segmentation

Voice

  • Whisper (base): speech-to-text
  • Phonon-31M-EN: text-to-speech

On-Device Training

  • LoRA and DiReFT fine-tuning for Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 0.5B and Qwen3 0.6B, aimed at personalized assistants and domain adaptation on-device

[Figure 3: ExecuTorch WebGPU demonstration]

Try it: ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground

The ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground runs many of the models above, all on the same WebAssembly + WebGPU runtime. All the prompts, photos, camera frames and audio never leave your device. Each model’s Hugging Face repo includes the .pte files, a model card, and the exact export recipe.

What’s Next

The backend is still in early development. We’ll keep making the backend faster and more stable, and expand operator, data type, and model coverage.

Contributions / Feedback

 ExecuTorch is open source, and we’d love your contributions to the WebGPU backend. If something breaks or a model you care about isn’t supported, open an issue or reach us on the ExecuTorch Discord. Contributions are welcome too, whether that’s new operators, new models or performance improvements.

Learn more at ExecuTorch Documentation | ExecuTorch repo | WebGPU Backend

The post ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser appeared first on PyTorch.

item.title: Optimizing Muse Spark Open on TPU v7 with SGLang-TorchTPU
item.dc:creator: Haolin Fu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Junyan Xu, Wangyuan Zhang, Haoguang Cai, RadixArk Team
item.description:
TL;DR We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend. At the...

The post Optimizing Muse Spark Open on TPU v7 with SGLang-TorchTPU appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend. At the center is a megakernel: all 62 layers of a decode or verify step run as one Pallas program, and every weight load, KV read and cross-device transfer is pipelined behind compute. The rest of the work falls into three groups: faster decode steps (collective folding, a max-free attention loop that pipelines its KV chunks, an expert loop that keeps register spills off its common path, and DFlash2 speculative decoding), more KV cache per chip (sequence-on-lane KV layout in the megakernel, and L2 HiCache on TPU with session-aware eviction), and faster prefill (a fused MoE kernel and sequence parallelism).

  • Decode speed. The megakernel halves the time per output token for one or two concurrent requests, where it helps the most; the gain narrows as concurrency grows. Its verify step runs within 1.5–1.7× of the time it takes just to stream its weights from HBM.
  • AgentX. On the 1M-context version of SemiAnalysis’s agentic-coding benchmark, our curve runs from 433 output tokens/s per request at 6,101 tokens/s per chip to 25,906 tokens/s per chip at 95 tokens/s per request (Figure 1).

Results

Figure 1. InferenceX AgentX, 1M-context trace set: tokens per dollar against p90 interactivity. TPU v7: one host, four chips, FP8 compute with NVFP4 expert weights. GB200 (FP4) is shown as a baseline from InferenceX’s published results as of 2026-11-02. Costs are InferenceX’s external owning costs: $1.21 per TPU v7 chip-hour and $1.86 per GB200 GPU-hour.

AgentX is built from 393 opt-in Claude Code sessions. It replays their request lengths, prefix sharing between turns, tool pauses and subagent structure, with synthetic tokens in place of the original content. We run its 1M-context trace set, as the GB200 baseline does, where prompts reach about 990K tokens; models with shorter context windows run a version capped at 256K. Throughput counts input and output tokens. Every TPU point in Figure 1 finishes requests within 47 s at p90.

Background

The model

Muse Spark Open is Meta’s open-weights mixture-of-experts (MoE) [1] model, with 816B parameters in total and about 42B active per token.

  • 62 decoder layers, all of them MoE. Each layer routes every token to 8 of 256 experts.
  • Hybrid attention. 46 layers use sliding-window attention [2] over the last 2,048 tokens; the other 16 attend over the full context, up to 1M tokens. Attention has 128 query heads and 16 KV heads, each 64 wide.
  • NVFP4 experts. Expert weights are 4-bit, with one scale per 16 values, a microscaling format [3].

The hardware

One TPU v7 (Ironwood) host has four chips. Each chip packs two chiplets, each with one TensorCore and its own HBM, and frameworks expose each chiplet as a device, so a host has 8 devices. We shard the model 8 ways with tensor parallelism [4], one shard per device.

Figure 2. One TPU v7 chip, simplified from the architecture diagram in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation. The numbers are Google’s published figures.

Each device is a single-threaded processor: one program runs at a time, so speed comes from keeping the matrix units fed and overlapping memory transfers with compute inside that program. These are the units that matter in this post, as described in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation and JAX’s Pallas TPU guide:

  • Scalar unit. One per device, with its own small scalar memory (SMEM). It runs the control flow: loops, branches and address math.
  • MXU, the matrix unit. Two per device. They do the matmuls; the chip’s peak is 2,307 TFLOPs in bf16 and 4,614 in fp8. At small batch they mostly wait for weights to arrive from HBM.
  • Vector unit (VPU). Elementwise work such as norms, softmax exponentials and format conversions. On recent TPUs it computes on 2D vector registers of 8 × 128 32-bit values, 8 sublanes by 128 lanes, so a data layout that leaves lanes empty wastes both vector work and memory (section 7). A cross-lane unit (XLU) next to it does transposes and permutes.
  • VMEM. On-chip SRAM next to the MXUs and the vector unit, with much higher bandwidth than HBM. Kernels stage their tiles here, so its size bounds how much a kernel can keep in flight.
  • DMA engines. They move data between HBM, VMEM and other devices in the background: a kernel starts a copy and waits for it later, while it computes. The megakernel’s pipelining (section 2) is built on them.
  • HBM. 192 GiB per chip at 7.37 TB/s, 96 GiB of it on each device.
  • Die-to-die link. It joins the two devices of a chip; Google documents it as six times faster than a 1D ICI link. Section 8’s pair exchange leans on it.
  • ICI. Six links per chip at 200 GB/s each, counting both directions, for 1,200 GB/s per chip. The four chips of a host talk to each other over it; slices of 64 chips or more form 3D tori.
  • Host. Each chip connects to the host’s CPUs over PCIe Gen5 ×16. A 4-chip host has 960 GB of DRAM, which L2 HiCache uses as a second cache tier (section 7).
  • SparseCores. Four per chip. This work does not use them.

The TorchTPU post has a longer primer.

The software

The server is SGLang-TorchTPU: SGLang’s [5] scheduler, KV cache and model code in PyTorch, with Pallas kernels on the hot paths. We decode with speculative decoding [6, 7]: a small draft model guesses the next few tokens, and the full model checks them all in one forward pass, the verify step. Each (request, position) pair in a verify step is a row, so two requests verifying 8 tokens each make a 16-row step.

1. A megakernel

At small batch, generating a token does little math per weight, so the step is as fast as HBM can stream the weights, as long as nothing interrupts the stream. A decode or verify step should therefore be one uninterrupted stream of weights from HBM into the MXU. Our previous path (“native” below) ran each layer as several kernels plus collectives, and every boundary stopped the stream. The megakernel runs all 62 layers of a step as one Pallas program per device, so the next weights are always in flight. Whole-step megakernels have been built for GPUs [8, 9] and, on TPU v7, for Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 [10]. Ours runs inside SGLang’s serving path, on its paged KV cache, for the decode and DFlash2 verify steps of many requests at once.

The native path was already built from fused Pallas blocks, yet its verify step took 2.9× the time needed to stream its weights. Profiling our first one-kernel prototype showed why: at batch 1 the matmuls and attention cost almost nothing, while collectives cost about 45 µs per layer. Nothing overlaps across a program boundary, so the step was bound by overhead, not by bandwidth.

Figure 3. One step. Inside the megakernel every layer runs the same flow (white); the shaded boxes are data movement the kernel issues itself.

For each step, every device runs one pallas_call that covers all 62 layers and the final norm. SGLang still runs the embedding, the draft model, a small KV-write kernel, the LM head and sampling around it.

Figure 4. Time per verify step, both paths with DFlash2 speculative decoding (GSM8K, measured on an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint). The floor is the time to stream that step’s distinct experts and dense weights from HBM.

Per output token, the megakernel is 1.94× faster than the native path for a single request (1.95 ms against 3.78 ms) and 1.85× for two concurrent requests. The next sections show what made one program this fast.

2. Pipelining everything inside the megakernel

A step is mostly data movement: weights, KV cache and partial sums between devices. Once the whole step is one program, the kernel can schedule every transfer so that it lands just before the compute that needs it [11], including across layer boundaries [10]. Figure 5 sketches one layer.

Figure 5. One layer of a step, schematic. Each DMA stream runs ahead of, or alongside, the compute that consumes it.

Weights arrive before they are needed

  • A ring for dense weights. Attention, o-proj and router weights stream through a ring of tiles that prefetches across layer boundaries. About ten tiles in flight sustain 3.34 TB/s per device, while a single DMA stream reaches only 1.13 TB/s.
  • Experts as soon as routing finishes. The router’s choice is known only mid-layer, so the kernel requests each chosen expert’s weights the moment routing ends, with three experts in flight.
  • The next layer during the expert loop. Refills for the next layer’s attention weights are held until the expert loop runs, so they never compete with the expert weights the current layer is waiting for.

Collectives leave as soon as their data exists

Tensor parallelism exchanges partial sums between the 8 devices several times per layer. Instead of a separate collective after each matmul, the kernel writes partial results straight into the owning device’s memory with remote DMAs issued from inside the kernel; a small round costs about 3 µs.

  • Streamed o-proj. Each o-proj output tile leaves for its owner as soon as it is computed, while the next tile is still being multiplied.

Pipelined KV writes

Each step writes its new K and V rows into the cache. In our fp8 sequence-on-lane cache (section 7), a token is one lane column of a 256-token page, so writing a token means reading the whole page block into VMEM, merging the new columns, and writing the page back.

This runs as a small kernel right after the megakernel, because XLA copies the aliased operands of any kernel that issues remote DMA. It used to do every page in turn: read, wait, merge, write, wait, for each request and each of 62 layers.

Figure 6. Schematic. The pipelined kernel issues all of a layer’s page reads at once, merges each page as it lands, and starts its write; the next layer’s reads start immediately on a second VMEM bank.

The new kernel loads all layers’ new rows once, then keeps two VMEM banks: layer l reads into one while layer l−1’s writes drain from the other, and a bank is reused only after the writes of two layers earlier have landed. The write cost per step fell from 810 to 155 µs at 16 rows and from 2,286 to 336 µs at 64 rows, with bit-identical results.

3. Collective folding

Because each layer is split across 8 devices, a device often has to collect the others’ results before it can continue. After the MoE and after attention, each device holds one slice of the layer’s output along the hidden dimension, and must all-gather the other seven slices before the next matvec can run. Collective folding lets that matvec start on the slices as they arrive instead of waiting for the whole gather, as decomposed collective matmuls do [12], here across the RMS norm that sits between the two.

Figure 7. Schematic. The folded matvec multiplies each gathered slice as soon as it lands, starting with the device’s own, and applies the per-row normalization at the end.

What makes this possible is where Muse Spark normalizes. The next layer’s attention input is an RMS norm [13] of the residual stream α·x + β·s·f, where x is the residual this device already holds, f is the gathered MoE output and s is f’s own norm factor. The two norm factors, s and the final r, are each one scalar per row. Scalars per row commute with the matmul, so the projection splits into a part the device can compute right away and a part that adds up slice by slice:

Here g is the norm’s gain vector, f_d is the slice from device d, and W_d is the matching block of weight rows. The kernel stacks the local part and the arriving slice into one product per block, consumes the slices in a fixed peer order, and reorders the weight ring so that W’s blocks stream in the same order. Once the last slice is in, it computes s and r and scales the result.

The kernel folds two all-gathers per layer this way: the MoE output into the next layer’s qkv projection, and the attention output into the pooler and router. The residual stream itself is unchanged; only the point where the matmul input is rounded to bf16 moves, so results are not bit-identical, and our accuracy checks cover it.

4. Enabling better pipelining in attention

At long context, attention is the largest part of a step. The kernel walks the KV cache chunk by chunk, and the key bottleneck was the running max of online softmax [14]: it chained every chunk to the one before, so chunks could not be pipelined.

The running max chains every chunk

Online softmax, as used by FlashAttention [15], keeps the maximum score seen so far. Each new chunk computes its scores, updates that maximum, exponentiates against it, and rescales everything accumulated so far whenever the maximum grows. So each chunk is a serial chain (wait for its DMA, QK, max, exp, sum, P·V, rescale) that cannot start its exponentials until the previous chunk’s maximum is known. In a microbenchmark this chain costs about 0.17 µs per chunk, whether the chunk is fp8 or bf16.

Muse Spark makes the max unnecessary

Muse Spark normalizes q and k (QK-norm [16, 17]) with an RMS norm that has no learned weight, and gives q a fixed gain. No attention score can exceed 43.8 in magnitude, far from where exp overflows in f32. The running max exists only to prevent that overflow, so the kernel drops it, along with the rescale. It checks the bound from the model’s constants when it is built. FlashDecoding++ [18] breaks the same chain on GPUs with a unified max value and a recomputation path for the rare overflow; here the bound is exact, so the kernel needs no fallback.

Figure 8. Schematic. With a running max, each chunk’s chain waits on the previous chunk. Without it, chunks are independent and their stages overlap.

Independent chunks pipeline

Without the max, chunks no longer depend on each other. The kernel issues all DMA waits at the top of each loop iteration, splits the chunks across several independent softmax streams that merge at the end, as Flash-Decoding does across the KV sequence [19], and software-pipelines the loop [11]: it scores the next chunks while it multiplies the previous chunks’ probabilities by V.

Three smaller changes shorten each chain further:

  • Chunk size by layer type. Global layers read the cache in long chunks of 1,024 to 2,048 tokens, so a 100K context needs far fewer chains. Sliding-window layers use 512-token chunks, since their window spans only a few.
  • fp8 keys straight into the MXU. Widening each fp8 chunk to bf16 on the vector unit cost more vector work than the MXU work it fed. Mixed bf16 × fp8 dots are exact, so the keys now go in as fp8.
  • The attention scale in the queries. Muse Spark’s attention scale is 1/8, a power of two, so multiplying the queries once instead of every score is exact.

Figure 9. Microbenchmark at production shapes. The memory floor is the time to read the KV bytes.

In the microbenchmark, longer chunks with independent streams cut attention time 2.4×, and dropping the running max took it to 3.9×. In the server, the pipelined loop raised per-request decode speed by 18% for two requests at 500K context.

5. Keeping register pressure off the common path

A processor computes on values held in its registers, a small, fixed set of storage slots next to the arithmetic units. When code needs more live values than the registers hold, the compiler spills some of them to memory and loads them back later [20], and those extra stores and loads cost time on every pass through the code. In a loop with several branches, the compiler has to fit the live values of all branches into the same registers, so one heavy branch can make every pass through the loop spill, even when that branch never runs.

The megakernel’s expert loop had exactly this problem. A step loops over the experts its rows were routed to. For each one, the kernel waits for the expert’s weights and runs a path chosen by how many rows the expert serves: a few-row path, with small variants for one to eight rows, and a dequantize-then-multiply path for busier experts. As the batch grows, a step visits more experts, but most of them still serve only one or two rows, so the light path is the one that matters.

One heavy branch slows the light path

The 8-row variant keeps large f32 accumulators that do not fit in the vector registers even on their own. Because it shared one loop body with the one- and two-row variants, the common path spilled registers to memory and loaded them back on every expert: about 0.37 µs per expert, against roughly 1.2 µs to stream that expert’s weights. That overhead had nothing to do with the work the light path itself did.

Two loops instead of one

The fix keeps the heavy code out of the light path’s loop. The kernel sorts a step’s experts by row count and runs two loops: one for experts with at most four rows, and one for the rest. Each loop body now holds only its own variants, so the few-row loop carries 61–64% fewer spill instructions. Every expert still takes the same path as before, so the output is bit-identical.

Figure 10. Schematic. In one shared loop body, every few-row expert is followed by a spill and refill, and the loop falls behind its weight stream. In their own loop, few-row experts keep pace with the weights.

In a kernel test with random routing, decode steps with many requests got 13–19% faster, and the expert loop now keeps pace with its weight stream.

6. Speculative decoding with DFlash2

Without speculation, every output token costs one full pass over the active weights. DFlash [21] drafts a whole block of tokens in one forward pass of a small model; we use Muse Spark’s DFlash2 draft model.

Figure 11. One speculative step. The draft model reads hidden states captured from the full model. The token strip is an illustration.

The draft attends bidirectionally within its block and proposes all of the block’s tokens at once. The full model checks the whole block in one megakernel step and keeps the longest prefix of drafts that matches its own choices, plus one token of its own.

This suits TPU well: MXU time grows with the number of row and output tiles, not with multiply-adds, and a block’s few rows fit in the same row tile as one token, so verifying a block costs little more than verifying one token. Measured on GSM8K with real acceptance, DFlash2 cut the megakernel’s time per output token for a single request from 3.93 to 1.95 ms, 2.0×.

7. More context per device: KV layout and L2 HiCache

On agent traffic, KV capacity is throughput: every prefix that falls out of the cache comes back as a 100K-token re-prefill. After the weights, each device has only about 20 GiB left for KV, split between a full-attention pool for the 16 global layers and a sliding-window pool for the other 46.

fp8 KV in a sequence-on-lane layout

Each device holds 2 of the 16 KV heads, each 64 values wide: half of a vector register’s 128 lanes. A token-major cache packs a head’s K and V side by side to fill the lanes. That works in bf16, but fp8 [22] packs four values per 32-bit word down the sublanes, so a K-and-V pair is padded to four slots and switching to fp8 alone saves nothing.

KV bytes per token, per layer, per device bf16 fp8
Token-major, K and V packed per head 512 B 512 B
Sequence-on-lane 512 B 256 B

The sequence-on-lane layout puts a page’s tokens along the 128 lanes and the head dimension down the sublanes, so each word holds four fp8 values of one token and nothing is padded. It halves both the KV memory and the KV bytes each step reads. Google engineers added this layout to SGLang-TorchTPU’s ragged paged attention kernel (#344), which serves prefill here, and the TorchTPU post describes it for Qwen 3.5. We rewrote the megakernel’s attention reads and its KV writes for it.

The draft model’s KV in the sliding-window pool

The draft model only attends to the last 2,048 tokens, but the server allocated its KV for the full context, almost a third of all KV memory per cached token. Serving it from the sliding-window pool lets the same HBM hold 38% more tokens.

L2 HiCache on TPU

We enabled SGLang’s hierarchical cache (HiCache) [23] on TPU, with host DRAM as an L2 behind every HBM pool: full-attention, sliding-window and draft. When HBM evicts a session’s prefix during a tool pause, its pages stay in host memory and are copied back on the next turn instead of being recomputed, as in multi-turn KV caching systems such as CachedAttention [24]. Making it work alongside speculative decoding and the overlap scheduler needed a new synchronization fence. On agent traffic, the L2 cache raised throughput by up to 77%.

Session-aware eviction

Agent traffic brought a second problem: the cache did not know which old prefixes would be needed again. An agent session is a tree of conversations: a main agent can sit idle for a quarter of an hour while its sub-agents run, then come back with its whole context. To plain LRU eviction, that idle conversation looks like the coldest data in the cache, so it goes first, and its next turn recomputes a long prefix. A hybrid model makes the loss worse: reusing a prefix needs both its full-attention KV and the sliding-window KV of its last 2,048 tokens, so losing only the small window makes the large full-attention KV useless. On this trace, prefill computed about 1.2× the tokens that the best possible cache would.

Figure 12. Schematic. A main agent idles while its sub-agents run. Plain LRU evicts its KV first; session-aware eviction keeps it in host memory until everything else has gone.

SGLang’s session-aware radix cache [5] (sgl-project/sglang#29173) gives the cache that knowledge. Requests from the same conversation share a session id, and KV that a live session will reuse is evicted only after everything else. We adapted it to agent traffic: the session id comes from the per-conversation id the client already sends, and the protection applies only in host memory, so HBM stays plain LRU for the requests that are running while host memory holds the idle conversations. In the highest-throughput run of Figure 1, prefill now computes within 1–5% of what the best possible cache would.

8. Prefill: a fused MoE kernel and fair batching

Before a request can start decoding, the server runs its new prompt tokens through the model in chunks of 4,096 tokens [25, 26]: the prefill. A chunk has enough rows to keep the matrix unit busy, so unlike decode, prefill time goes to compute and to moving results between devices. On agent traffic a single turn can bring hundreds of thousands of new tokens, so prefill speed decides how long requests wait before their first token.

In the MoE layers of prefill, every device computes a partial result for every (token, expert) pair, and each token’s owner must add up 8 of them. Moving those partials, one small write at a time, cost more than the matrix math.

The fused MoE kernel and the pair exchange

Experts are sharded with tensor parallelism: each device holds 1/8 of every expert. Each device therefore runs every (token, expert) row of a prefill chunk against its slice, producing a full-width partial per row; Muse Spark normalizes each expert’s output before the weighted sum, so a row’s 8 partials must all be added up before its owner can apply the norm and combine experts. The kernel streams one expert’s weights while the next prefetches, runs gate/up, SwiGLU [27] and down, and writes each finished row straight into its owner’s HBM, overlapping later tiles.

Figure 13. The two devices on a chip share a die-to-die link, which Google documents as six times faster than a 1D ICI link to another chip.

Each row’s write took about 50 ns of scalar work on the same unit that issues the matmuls, so writes serialized with compute. The pair exchange uses the chip’s topology instead. Each device sends its whole tile to its sibling on the same chip over the fast on-chip link, and the pair’s sum then goes to each remote owner once, as one DMA per contiguous run of rows. Cross-chip bytes halve, each owner adds 5 blocks instead of 8, and the MoE kernel went from 3,247 to 2,368 µs per layer.

Smaller changes trimmed the rest of the path:

  • Weight ping-pong. Alternating two weight buffers lets each expert’s fetch start while the previous expert computes.
  • A one-pass combine. The owner’s sum of partials, per-expert norm and weighted sum ran as three XLA passes; one fused Pallas pass reads the partials once.
  • No zero fill, unrolled writes. Every output row is written exactly once, so the zero fill of the output buffer was dropped, and the per-row DMA loop issues 8 rows per iteration.

Together with these smaller changes, the pair exchange cut a 4,096-token prefill chunk from 440 to 384 ms on a cold 100K-token prompt.

Sequence-parallel prefill

Tensor parallelism splits every matmul across the 8 devices, but each device still holds the activations of the whole chunk, so the per-token work between the matmuls, such as norms, residual updates and routing, is repeated on every device. Sequence parallelism [28] splits the tokens instead: between layers, each device keeps only its own 512 of the chunk’s 4,096 tokens. The norms and residual updates then run on an eighth of the tokens, and attention’s all-reduce becomes a reduce-scatter, which delivers each device only its own tokens’ sums. Routing packs each token’s expert ids and weights into one small all-gather. The MoE output reaches its tokens’ devices through an all-to-all: each device receives only its own tokens’ columns from the other seven, an eighth of the bytes of the all-gather it replaces, which sent every device the columns of all 4,096 tokens. This cut a 4,096-token forward at 131K context by 51 ms, about 11%. It changes the order of some reductions, so results are not bit-identical, and our accuracy checks cover it.

Chunk sharing

A cold prompt of hundreds of thousands of tokens is prefilled in 4,096-token chunks of about half a second each. The scheduler used to give every chunk to that prompt until it finished, so other turns’ few thousand new tokens waited 15 to 95 s behind it.

Figure 14. Schematic. The long prompt keeps at least 1,024 tokens of each batch, waiting turns fill the rest, and the long prompt finishes a little later.

Now a prompt in the middle of a chunked prefill keeps at least 1,024 tokens of each batch, and waiting turns fill the rest. In an AgentX test, this cut median end-to-end latency by 58% and p90 by 33%, with throughput within 5%.

Future work

  • Attention closer to the memory floor, by packing the 64-wide heads to fill the MXU and shortening the per-chunk chain further.
  • A topology-aware MoE layout, with expert parallelism across chips and tensor parallelism inside each chip, to make most of the MoE exchange local.
  • Faster prefill, now the limit at high concurrency, through larger prefill graphs, collectives overlapped with compute and a reworked MoE prefill kernel.
  • Prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation, optimizing AgentX performance with prefill and decode on separate hosts.
  • Upstreaming this work into SGLang-TorchTPU’s main branch.

Code

Everything here is open source in SGLang-TorchTPU, branch haolin/ms-v11. The megakernel lives in sglang_tpu/muse_megakernel/, the fused MoE prefill kernel in sglang_tpu/moe/pallas/fused_rs/.

item.content:encoded:
The Call for Proposals for PyTorch Day China 2026 closes November 10 at 23:59 China Standard Time. The event takes place in Beijing on December 12, bringing together PyTorch developers, machine learning engineers, AI researchers, and open source AI leaders from across China and beyond.

The call welcomes session presentations and lightning talks across five topic areas:

  • Model Training & Post-Training: Distributed training, SFT, reinforcement learning, preference optimization, and techniques for improving training efficiency and performance.
  • Efficient Inference & Deployment: LLM inference, quantization, optimization, deployment strategies, and production-ready AI solutions.
  • PyTorch Core & Hardware Acceleration: Compilation, kernel optimization, performance profiling, and GPU and AI accelerator technologies.
  • Physical AI: Robotics, intelligent devices, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, perception and control systems, and simulation-based training.
  • PyTorch Ecosystem & Applications: Tools, applications, and innovations expanding the PyTorch ecosystem.

CFP notifications are scheduled for November 17, followed by the schedule announcement on November 18.

Submit a proposal by November 10 at 23:59 China Standard Time.

item.title: KVCache Meetup Korea 2026: Event Recap

item.description:

The post KVCache Meetup Korea 2026: Event Recap appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
On the evening of Sep 30, 2026, PyTorchKR and XCENA co-hosted KVCache Meetup Korea. PyTorchKR is a major AI/ML community in Korea, and XCENA is a startup that focuses on CXL (Compute Express Link). Tensormesh, the company behind LMCache, also sponsored the event. Speakers from XCENA, SK hynix, FuriosaAI, and LMCache shared their work on large language model (LLM) inference and KV Cache optimization. LLM inference runs a language model to generate output. KV Cache stores attention data for reuse during inference.

 
Attendees at KVCache Meetup Korea 2026.

Talks covered CXL memory expansion, GPU and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bottlenecks, request scheduling on RNGD, and LMCache MP Mode. The sessions showed how hardware and serving software handle KV Cache in different ways. Serving software processes requests that run a model.

Registration and Opening

The program combined technical talks with opportunities for attendees to connect. Attendees who wanted to join the networking chose up to two interest stickers at registration. The five categories were Model, Serving, Infra, Hardware, and Memory.

 
Attendees chose their interest stickers at registration.

PyTorchKR organizer Junghwan Park and XCENA CPO Juhyun Kim opened the event. The speakers were Jooho Lee from XCENA, Sejin Oh from SK hynix, Donghun Lee from FuriosaAI, and Baoloong Mao from LMCache. They shared their experiences and approaches.

   
Junghwan Park from PyTorchKR (left) and Juhyun Kim, CPO at XCENA (right), welcomed the attendees.

CXL and KV Cache Storage: Jooho Lee, XCENA

The session “CXL for KVCache” started with the basics of CXL and memory expansion. Jooho Lee explained how CXL expands the memory space that CPUs can access with load/store instructions. He also described a setup where multiple hosts use a memory pool and introduced Maru. Maru is a high-performance KV Cache storage engine that XCENA released as an open-source project. It helps LLM inference use shared CXL memory efficiently.


Jooho Lee from XCENA presented “CXL for KVCache.”

The KV Cache design combined DRAM and SSD storage in a CXL memory pool. It kept frequently used cache in DRAM and less frequently used cache on SSDs. Maru connects the inference engine to these storage layers. Optimizing LLM inference requires more than storing a large amount of cache. The path and cost of moving cache to the GPU also matter.

The talk also covered splitting computation for experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models between a GPU and MX1. Experts are specialized parts of a model. The design places some weights in memory near MX1 and processes them there. It transfers intermediate values, called activations, and computation results instead of the full weights. The session started with KV Cache storage and also covered weight placement and ways to reduce data movement.

GPU Compute and HBM Bandwidth: Sejin Oh, SK hynix

Sejin Oh presented “Analyzing Utilization of GPU and HBM in LLM Serving Systems.” The talk examined how prefill and decode use system resources. Prefill processes the prompt, and decode generates output tokens. The session presented Roofline analysis alongside measurements from a running system. Roofline analysis compares compute and memory bandwidth limits.


Sejin Oh from SK hynix presented the analysis of GPU compute and HBM bandwidth.

The experiments used two H100 GPUs, Llama 3.1 8B, and vLLM. GPU compute use was high during the main projection operations in prefill. During decode, HBM bandwidth use was high. The experiments also explained the difference between TTFT and TPOT. TTFT measures the time to the first output token. TPOT measures the time per output token.

Reusing KV Cache reduces computation during prefill. After that reduction, memory bandwidth can become the bottleneck. Whether a service needs more memory capacity or bandwidth depends on its input and output lengths, batch size, and other operating conditions.

Scheduling and KV Cache on RNGD: Donghun Lee, FuriosaAI

FuriosaAI is building Furiosa-LLM, its own inference engine for running LLMs on RNGD. In “LLM Inference Engine for RNGD,” Donghun Lee shared engineering problems from building the engine, including request scheduling and KV Cache management. He followed each request from arrival to execution. He explained PagedAttention for KV Cache blocks, Continuous batching for active requests, and Chunked prefill for smaller prompt segments. He also introduced buckets, or tensor shapes compiled before execution.


Donghun Lee from FuriosaAI explained how to share KV Cache outside a node.

Combining requests into one batch increases throughput, or the number of requests processed over time. Larger batches can need larger buckets and increase latency, or response delay. Furiosa-LLM measures the execution cost on the actual hardware. It merges two batches when the combined cost is lower than processing them separately. The decision also accounts for the context length of each request and the cost of padding. Padding fills unused positions in a fixed tensor shape.

The talk compared the benefit of cache reuse with the cost of transferring it. The slides used a 12,370-token prompt, with one request at a time and three measurements for each condition. Retrieving the host cache and generating the first token took about 92 ms. Recomputing the cache took about 900 ms. Under those test conditions, retrieving the host cache was faster. He also explained how to overlap cache transfer with computation at each layer.

The benefit depends on the amount of data transferred and the available bandwidth. Experimental features included a network-shared cache and running prefill and decode on separate resources. He also discussed plans for future expansion.

‘LMCache: A Unified KV Cache Management Layer with Multi-Platform Architecture’: Baoloong Mao, LMCache

LMCache maintainer and core architect Baoloong Mao presented “A Unified KV Cache Management Layer with Multi-Platform Architecture.” LMCache is an open-source KV Cache project created by the team that founded Tensormesh. He explained how LMCache connects different inference engines with storage systems and hardware. He focused on MP Mode, which moves cache management from inside the inference engine into a separate process.


Baoloong Mao from LMCache introduced the unified KV Cache layer and MP Mode.

In MP Mode, CUDA IPC allows processes to share GPU memory. IPC means communication between processes. The processes exchange control information such as block IDs. They use a shared CPU memory pool within a node to reduce duplicate storage. MP Mode also reads and loads data from several storage layers in parallel. This design separates inference computation from cache I/O, or data transfers, to reduce competition for resources.

The session also covered deployment and operations. Topics included deployment on Kubernetes and monitoring cache hit rates and cache lifetimes. A cache hit means that the requested data is available. The talk also covered isolating failures between inference and cache processes. External plugins allow connections to more storage systems and devices.

Q&A and Networking

In the Q&A session, the speakers returned to the stage to answer questions from attendees. Questions included separating prefill and decode, compared with mixed batching. Mixed batching processes prefill and decode work together. Attendees also asked about the roles of LMCache and the cache features built into vLLM. Another topic was the plan to extend MP Mode across multiple nodes.

         
The speakers answered live questions together after the talks.

After the Q&A, attendees from different fields gathered in small groups to talk. Their interest stickers helped them find people with similar interests. Speakers and attendees exchanged ideas and heard different perspectives.

Conversations also continued around the CXL server from XCENA at the venue. Attendees examined the hardware up close and asked questions. They linked the memory expansion techniques from the talks to the hardware on display.

 
Attendees talked during the networking session.

Feedback from 72 Survey Responses

The following summary draws on 72 survey responses. All numbers and percentages below use the survey responses as their base. Some questions allowed multiple selections.


Event satisfaction and work experience by role, based on 72 survey responses.

In the feedback questions, 48 respondents selected the program as a positive point (66.7%). The venue and facilities received 30 selections (41.7%). The atmosphere for conversations and the event timing each received 22 selections (30.6%). This question allowed multiple selections. Respondents gave positive feedback on the talks and the chance to meet other attendees.

Repeated comments mentioned microphone quality and volume, screen visibility from the back rows, and limited space. Some respondents also asked for interpretation or translation to help them follow the English talks. Some respondents also asked for a dedicated session where developers in the same field can talk. Requests for future events included real production examples, vLLM and SGLang internals, compilers for neural processing units (NPUs), recent inference optimization techniques, and demos. Respondents wanted details about problems, trial and error, and solutions from real deployments. They asked speakers to explain these experiences, as well as their products.


Group photo from KVCache Meetup Korea.

PyTorchKR will use this feedback to plan and run future events. Thank you to everyone who joined the event on a weekday evening. The organizers also thank the speakers who shared their knowledge and experience. Thank you to PyTorchKR and XCENA for organizing the event, and to Tensormesh for its support.
